Rudolph has been in charge of the Mentor homestead during the President's absence, and has had care of the President's two younger sons, aged respectively 9 and 11 years. In obedience to a telegram last night from Mrs. Garfield, these children are left at Mentor. They were informed last evening of the President's almost hopeless condition, and were greatly distressed, but did not murmur on being told they could not go to him.

Want to Lynch Him.

* DENVER, August 26.—A News South Arkansas special says: The body of a man named McCorkey was found at Mears last night. Evidence points strongly to Charles Stone, a notorious desperado, as his murderer. Stone came over to South Arkansas shortly after the murder and was arrested. A number of McCorkey's friends came after him, but the officials spirited him away. Fifty armed men are to-night scouring the streets looking for the murderer, with the intention of lynching him.

Vice President Arthur.

New York, August 26.—Vice President Arthur was seen at his home to-day at noon. He has only received the official bulletins in regard to the President's condition. He has not been summoned, nor has he received any intimation to be in readiness to go to the Capital. Should he receive such a message he would go at once. He refuses to state what he thought of the President's condition or its requirements in relation to the Vice President.

A Fusion.

JACKSON (Miss.), August 26.—The Republicans have ratified the Greenback nominations, and agreed on a fusion ticket as follows: Benjamin King, Governor; J. B. Yellowby, Lieutenant King, Governor; J. B. Yellowby, Lieutenant Governor, J. K. Shellman (colored), Secretary of State; W. H. Bynam, Treasurer; A. T. Wimberly, Auditor; W. F. Fitzgerald, Attorney General; W. D. House, Superintendent of Education. A joint mass mass meeting was held last night and was presided over over by John K. Lynch (colored).

St. Louis, August 26.—A Republican Lexington, Mo., special says: An omnibus, which was conveying passengers from the Wabash railroad to Lexington, about 8 o'clock this evening, was entered by four heavily armed and masked men, who robbed the passengers, five in number of all their money, watches and other valuables, and then escaped. A posse of men has gone in pursuit of the robbers.

Another Officer Killed.

Denver, Aug. 27.—At Silverton late last night D. C. Ogsburg, City Marshal, was killed by two roughs, Burt Wilkinson and Dyson H. Bridge. The whole town is aroused and the murderers will be lynched if captured. Bridge is a notorious deser-
perado, and large rewards are offered for his arrest for other crimes.

TEXAS TOP1C8.
Giddings is now shipping on an average about sixty bales of cotton a day.
Columbus is working manfully to get the workshops of the San Antonio railway.
Comanche county has only seven camp meetings going on now; more are wanted.
An Austin saloon sells beer at 10 cents a glass. The Houston Age made the discovery.
The total assessments of Bexar county including the city of San Antonio is $10,558,987.
The Sunset road has presented the Columbus oil mills with a pair of $800 railroad scales.
Immigrants are passing through Clarendon every week going up into the Pan Handle counties.
John T. Collier, one of Houston county's best citizens, was killed by lightning a few days ago.
A cotton exchange has been organized at Columbus, and B. M. Baker, of the Citizen, is a member.
It is expected that the new Baptist church at Giddings will be dedicated about the last of September.
Judge J. M. Conatter, 61 years of age, and Mrs. Hart, aged 51, were married a few days ago at Baird.

Two Chinamen are about starting a laundry in Belton; such an establishment is needed, says the Courier.

The Belton Journal of the 25th reports Mr. Farley, the wounded drummer, as still in a critical condition.

Mr. James Harris, an old and highly respected citizen of Palo Pinto county, died of measles a few days ago.

San Antonio has five banks and many wealthy men, yet the assessment rolls show but $92,580 money on hand.

The anniversary meeting of the Palo Pinto Baptist association will be held at Slaughter valley church tomorrow.

McLennan county has no complaint to make of her officers—they are fearless and impartial in the discharge of their duty.

J. L. Britton, of Mexia, was found dead on the road fifteen miles from Floresville. He is supposed to have died from thirst.

The Denison Herald-News now runs a temperance column, but we believe it makes no pretensions to be a prohibition paper.

It is generally conceded that corn left over from last year is in much better condition than usually is the case—being free of weevil.

Quite a lively time was had in Morris county last week in attempting to capture a lot of desperadoes, one of whom was killed.

The Bellville Times says cotton is coming in very fast and that trade is good. A car load of beer on ice is received and disposed of every week.

John Sumerston was arrested in LaSalle county on the charge of murdering McCoy, a deputy sheriff of Gonzales county some months ago.

The Austin Statesman's local reporter is moonstruck. He watches the moon and tells his readers to turn the money over in their pockets for luck.

Corsicana is looking up rapidly, owing to its recently increased railroad facilities, as twenty-six new brick buildings are now in course of construction there.

The latest news from Orange is that all is quiet; that Delno is released on a $2000 bond and that he and the Harrises are all getting ready to leave the country.

The San Antonio Light complains of the small assessment of money and personal property of Bexar county and says that they are all as poor as Job's turkey.
George Williams, a colored brakeman on the Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe railroad, was killed near Rosenburg junction a few days ago by falling from the moving train.

If the weather continues favorable abou two-thirds of a crop of cotton will be gatht ered in Austin county. Farmers are paying sixty cents per 100 pounds for picking.

In the recorder's court at San Antonio the other day, the prosecuting witness in a fight case testified that the defendant has struck him over 2,000 times in less than a minute.

The LaGrange Journal boasts over two bales of cotton hauled from within two miles of Flatonia. It says LaGrange is receiving plenty of cotton and selling plenty of goods.

Corsicana now glories in a cotton exchange. A county cotton exchange consists simply of a combination of cotton buyers for the purpose of obtaining the market reports at reduced rates.

Judge Murdock and his family were living in a large tent near Clarendon, and a few days ago, while the entire family was absent, the heat of the sun ignited an open box of matches in the tent, destroying it and its contents.
Waco is still exercised over the mystery of the identity of the man Castello who suicided at Corsicana a few days ago, as there is a chain of evidence to establish the fact that the man was Chas. W. Beach, a Mississippi lawyer of that city.

A locomotive tender on the Gulf, Colorado & Santa Fe railroad tumbled into the turn table pit at Brenham a few days ago. Nothing was broken, but there was considerable trouble to get it out and several railroad men did some tall swearing.

A case of wholesale poisoning is reported in the vicinity of Kaufman. The family of a Mrs. Smith and her tenants—ten in all—were poisoned by eating cooked peaches containing arsenic. At last accounts all were in a dangerous condition.

Four Mexican horse thieves were murdered near Brackett while in charge of two men named McLoed and Thompson, who claim that the men were killed by a crowd. The jury of inquest returned a verdict that the Mexicans were killed by persons unknown.

The San Antonio Evening Light describes a character that it calls the "drunk roller." He is a man that follows up strangers he duds drinking and when the stranger is drunk, down and asleep in some secluded
unds drinking and when the stranger is drunk, down and asleep in some secluded spot rolls him over and goes through his pockets. The Giddings Lone Star reports the result of a camp hunt thus: They remained out several days; killed a good many squirrels and saw a good many that they didn't kill.
brockett-brockett-1881-08-26.A9:
The Statesman's Specials.
following from Brackett, Texas, says: "Our town was thrown into a fever of excitement this morning, caused by the report that four horse thieves, all Mexicans, had been killed by some unknown parties while being brought to town to be lodged in jail. It appears that a few days ago three or four sheep men, McLeod and Thompson were deputized to arrest these thieves, a regular organized band of whom had started along the Rio Grande, and for some time have been running off stock from many parts of the county. Immediately after being deputized the gentlemen pursued and overtook the rascals, capturing four of them, whom they were bringing back to town in an ambulance, and had gotten within about twelve miles of here and near the town of Dolores, when they were rushed upon by some hidden parties, who commenced firing and succeeded in killing all four of the thieves. One of the men killed, named Tolomantez, is well known throughout this section of the country as a desperado and horse thief. Upon receiving information of the killing Justice Maguire summoned a jury, and went out to hold an inquest over the bodies, but has not yet returned."

This evening some of the Seminole scouts arrived in town, bringing with them about twelve head of horses, captured from a man who was driving them off when the Seminoles came up to him. He rode away, leaving the horses to them. The Seminoles immediately rounded them up and drove them to town.

Comanche, August 25.—We were yesterday blessed with a good rain, which will be a great benefit to crops.

Cotton picking going on rapidly, and prospects for heavy fall business.

We only have seven campmeetings going on now in Comanche county.

Old man Payne, the murderer of Wm. Woods, at Sipe Springs, is still at large, and Sheriff Yates, in pursuit, is determined to bring him to justice.

Comanche is determined to support Galveston for the medical department of the university, and either Waco or Thorp Springs for the literary department.

Col. W. H. H. Lawrence, of the Fort Worth and Rio Grande railroad, is in Comanche, and our people are alive to the interest of this road.

The district court meets the first week in September. There are several important murder cases to be disposed of.

We learn that Mrs. Allen, who was so badly burned by kerosene explosion last week, is not dead. Her daughter, who was burned into a crisp, died immediately.

Our mail between Comanche and Dublin, on the Central road, is so irregular that very few would regret a change of carriers.

Liberty Hill, August 25.—Mr. John Russell, one of our best citizens, met with a sad accident this morning. His right arm was caught and badly crushed by a band attached to his steam gin. He is 86 years old. It is probable that he will recover.

Business is increasing as new cotton is brought in to market. Stock are doing well, though rain would improve the range.

TAYLOR, August 24.—Work was commenced at this place to-day on the extension of the Missouri and Pacific railroad.

Good rains are falling north of town, insuring a good winter range.

The citizens are making an effort to establish a graded school at Taylor, and most of the money necessary has already been subscribed.

LLANO, Texas, August 23.—Llano City is a prosperous and pretty place. Stock of all kinds looks well and merchants are doing a good business.

I have talked university in Blanco, Gillespie and Llano counties, and every man is for locating the university at Austin. No one wants division.

A good rain has fallen to-day.

The Llano river is low.

Three men charged with loving other men's cattle too well, were lodged in jail yesterday. This is fast becoming a farming as well as a stock country.

It is estimated that over 2,000 bales of cotton will be raised here this year.

WHITESBORO, August 27.—This little village is running up like magic. Three railroads intersect here, running a total of about twenty-five trains per day. The population of Whitesboro is nine hundred, or more.

Crops light

FORT WORTH, August 28.—Hon H. J. Labatt and Hon. James B. Stubbs, of Galveston, reached this city to-day, and intended to address the citizens to-night on the university question. Upon consultation with prominent citizens they have abandoned the idea, on account of the intense excitement over the president's condition.

They will leave for Tyler tomorrow.

Farmers report that the cotton crop will yield 700 or 800 pounds of seed cotton to the acre.

ed-reines-1881-08-17.A2:
Fools and Damphools.
The world has agreed for the sake of convenience to divide its fools into two species. One it calls simply a fool; the other, to adopt the word which Doesticks applied to his friend, it calls a damphool. This is used strictly in its scientific, not its profane, and has nothing in common with the shallow and random use which angry men make of it to give vent to their momentary irritation. It is as distinct and technical a label as "mustang" to describe a species of horse, or "terrier" to describe a species of dog.

A fool is often harmless, and may be snubbed and kept in order. A damphool cannot be. A fool is often tolerable and docile. If he cannot be taught much wisdom, he can be taught obedience and respect. But though a damphool may have intelligence, he has little or no reverence. A fool may have some humor, but a damphool has none. A tool can be made a fool of; a damphool makes a fool of himself. A fool may have a little sense, but whatever other sense a damphool may possess, he is sure to lack common sense. A fool may be humble and retiring, but it is the essence of his kinsmen to be conceited and self-asserting. A fool generally knows he is a fool, and so is often doleful when he thinks of it; but a damphool never knows it, and so is happy. A fool is often stupid, headless, blundering, aimless, like a hen or a fly; the other is strutting, irritating, conceited, like a turkey and a peacock; or a noisy nuisance, like a June beetle. A fool is often patient, well-digposed, and, though slow, good-natured, like the ass; but his foster brother is apt to bear malice, and is intelligently obstinate like the mule.

To the ranks of the odious kind of fool belong those who hanker morbidly for notoriety—the Tanners, the Bradlaughs, the Guiteaus, the Booths, the Count Johannes and George Francis Trains. Poor Train, however, has stepped down and out of the ranks, and now appears to be simply and only a fool. The fool is an object of sympathy, of pity, compassion and help; his robust relative gives cause for disgust, for sport, for derision and ridicule. Shakspeare, of course, saw the difference between these types, and has drawn them with his usual clearness and acuteness. His fools and clowns are famous—Touchstone and Dogberry; Launce, Slender old Gobbo, and the like; but his damphools—such as Justice Shallow, Pistol, Falstaff, Polonious, old Capulet, have equal rights to consideration. When, in the play of “Midsummer Night’s Dream,” the dramatist changed Bottom the Weaver into an ass, he turned his damphool into a simple fool. For Bottom the Weaver imagines he can write a play, take the chief role and be stage manager all at the same time, making himself poussed and ridiculous, indeed; but changed into an ass he is docile and humble and wants only to have his head scratched and to be fed on dried peas and good sweet hay.

A fool may be pious and reverential, believe in creeds and religion; but the other sort is quite likely to be an atheist. David undoubtedly meant to write that the damphool “hath said there is no God.”

GEORGIA’S TEMPERANCE BILL.—The general temperance bill, reported by the special committee, was defeated in the Georgia senate Tuesday by a vote of 20 to 19. Twenty-three votes were necessary to its passage.

A BRUTE LYNCHED.—A Paducah (Ky.) special says that on August 9 E. Reeves, colored, attempted indecent violence on the person of Miss Dora Lingston, in Graves county, having broken into the room in the night. Her cries brought help, and he fled. The whole country swarmed with pursuers. He was captured at Ogden’s Landing in Ballard county yesterday. To-day he was taken away by a large mounted mob from the persons conducting him to the Graves county jail and subsequently lynched.

STUDIES OF ROMAN CATHOLIC YOUTH.—A telegram from Cincinnati, Ohio, August 16, says:—Coadjutor Bishop Elder, of this diocese, has just completed arrangements for the reorganization of the parochial schools. The history of the United States and the Constitution are to be prominent studies, and especial attention will be given to the cultivation of good morals.

The boys of Westminister school had a remission or holiday to enable them to attend the funeral of Dean Stanley. Some of them took advantage of this to play cricket.

Lewis G. Folger, esq., of Cincinnati, was cured of neuralgia by St. Jacobs Oil.
ed-reines-1881-08-17.A3:
Criminal.
Ed. Reeves, a negro, was hung by lynchers in Bullard county, Ky., on Tuesday, for assault on a white woman.

Eight mer, supposed to be Molly Maguire murderers, have been captured by Pinkerton detectives near Uniontown, Pa.

Gum Yum, a young Chinaman, committed suicide in Napsonset river on Saturday evening, on account of homesickness.

Parties from Rosabud agency state that Spotted Tail was killed for seducing another Indian's squaw, and they say this was his 150th offence.

Mosher and Fuller of Western Sea notoriety were examined at Machias, Monday, and held for trial in $50,000 each. The prisoners seemed much depressed.

A dispatch from Montreal says it was reported that six men outraged three young girls just over the border in New York state, Friday, and that two of the victims died.

The Boston liquor squad raided on 29 unlicensed dealers, on Friday, and secured over two thousand gallons of the ardent. This is the largest seizure ever made at the hub.

Christiana Tyler, an old negro woman who was arrested for the murder of a little boy and girl, aged three and six years, respectively, on the farm of Joseph Fisher, on the Bunker Hill road, near Washington, has confessed that she committed the deed.

Gately, who was arrested at Dedham, Mass., for the murder of his wife, has made a confession, stating that she angered him and that he beat her with a stick, which he afterwards threw away. He did not intend to kill her, he says. They hang such fellows as he in Massachusetts.

A bloody double tragedy occurred at the town of Burton, Mo., on the Wabash railroad, on Wednesday. A man named Jackson insulted a lady named Langford. The lady told her husband, who at once hunted up Jackson, and began chastising him. Jackson drew a knife and stabbed Langford several times, inflicting mortal wounds. Mrs Langford then appeared on the scene and shot Jackson in the breast, whereupon he turned on the woman, cut her slightly two or three times, when he fell exhausted from loss of blood. Both Jackson and Langford will die.

Benjamin Bird (colored), convicted of the murder of Policeman Nelson (colored) June 25, 1880, during the mill riot at Jacksonville, Fla., was executed at 12 o'clock, Friday, in the jail yard. A short time previous to the execution he made a confession of the crime to the sheriff and others, but while on the gallows protested his innocence. When the trap was sprung and Bird fell, the noose had not been properly arranged, the end slipped out and he fell to the ground. He got up with the assistance of the sheriff, and again walked upon the trap, the rope being properly adjusted, and he was launched into eternity.

James and Walter Malley have been arrested at New Haven charged with the murder of Jennie E. Cramer, the young girl whose death has produced such a sensation in the city of elms. Blanche Douglass made a confession before the coroner's jury at Sheriff Peck's house, Tuesday night, regarding the death of Jennie Cramer. She says that on Friday night she was called into the room occupied by James Malley and Jennie Cramer, to quiet Jennie, who was screaming and pleading with James Malley. At midnight she was still in consultation with the jury, but nothing further was elicited. The citizens of Orange, in town meeting Tuesday afternoon, voted to offer a reward of $1000 for evidence enough to convict the murderer or murderess of Jennie Cramer.

The town of Dedham, Mass.. was the scene of a murder, Wednesday night. Patrick Gately and his wife, Mary, live in the east part of Dedham. Mrs Gately was the victim, and her husband's story is that she complained of feeling unwell, about 7:30 o'clock, and that she went to bed. Next foren o1, about 5 o'clock, he called her, but got no answer. He went into her room and found that the whole left side of her was crushed in and marks of violence all over her body. The bed was stained with blood, and there was evidence of a violent struggle. The walls and ceiling was also stained with blood. Her husband has been arrested for the crime, and the clothes that he wore have the appearance of having been washed. His handkerchief also contained brook sand. A medical examiner will hold an autopsy. Gately is about forty years old. There is great excitement. Gately protests his innocence.

N. H. N. G. Encampment.

The annual encampment of the first brigade of the New Hampshire National

N. H. N. G. Encampment.

The annual encampment of the first brigade of the New Hampshire National Guard will be held on the land of Mrs Rowe, about a mile north of West Concord village, just above the fork of the roads, commencing Tuesday, September 13, and continuing four days. The land which has been selected for the encampment is admirably adapted for the purpose. It consists of nearly 100 acres, is very level, gently sloping towards the river. The various companies will be requested to report at camp Monday evening, in order to be ready for duty early the next morning.

Supreme Court.

The following is the arrangement of the trial terms of New Hampshire's supreme court judges: Nashua, Sept. 6, Clark; Dover, Sept. 6, Allen; Newport, Sept. 6, Smith; Colebrook, Sept. 6, Carpenter; Luconia, Sept. 27, Carpener; Haverhill, Sept. 27, Blodgett; Concord, Oct. 4, Stanley; Lancaster, Oct. 11, Allen; Ossipee, Oct. 18, Blodgett; Portsmouth, Oct. 18, Smith; Keene, October 18, Carpenter; Plymouth, Nov. 1, Stanley.
ed-reines-1881-08-17.A4:
An invitation to attend the stock and agricultural fair to be held at Chicago in September from the 12th to the 17th inclusive, has been received by THE BULLETIN. The managers promise to make this the great live stock and agricultural fair of the United States, one worthy of Chicago and the northwest.

Only seven states in the Union have annual sessions of their legislatures, and some of them will probably soon move into the biennial line. The next reform should be the limitation of every legislative body to a forty-day session, and no pay to members if they stay a minute longer.

The cattle disease in Logan county still continues, without any remedy yet having been found. Animals become suddenly blind, and few of them recover. The cause is by some attributed to the dry weather and dust, and by others to a gadfly or miller, which lays eggs in the corner of the eye.

A bad fight over a dog occurred between two men in a down town saloon late last night. The fighters were Frie, the tailor, and Doering, the barber. They were seperated by the proprietor before any damage was done to either or to anything. A large crowd witnessed the affair which was decidedly ludicrous.

Ed. Reeves, the scoundrel who attempted to violate the person of Miss Dora Langston, in Graves county, Kentucky, about a week ago, was captured in Ballard county at the house of a man named Ford by Messrs. A. J. Cunn and Wm. Harper,
who shortly after turned him over to a party
of men who came by there in search of the
negro. It is believed that the men hung
the wretch to a tree before they left Ballard
county.

—Two little boys, aged about seven and
eight years respectively, were playing in the street on Washington avenue near Nineteenth street yesterday evening about four o'clock, when one of them was attacked by a ferocious bore hog. The beast grabbed the child in the calf of the leg and while lacerating it the other little fellow picked up a stick and rushed to the rescue when the beast suddenly turned upon him, caught his arm and buried his teeth in the flesh. The cries of the lads attracted the attention of passers by, and Mr. Eberly, who was among the first to notice the trouble, hurried to the assistance of the boys and rescued them from their perilous predicament. As it is, both boys received very painful wounds, but they might have been crippled for life. The beast should be hunted down and killed and the ordinance against bore hogs in general be rigidly enforced.

—The importance of Cairo as a United States hospital station has been recognized by the department at Washington and a gentleman from Baltimore, Maryland, an experienced pharmacist, has been ordered here to assist Dr. Carter in the management of the marine hospital. The monthly reports of the hospital here show that the amount of work done, the number of days of treatment furnished, and the number of patients treated, in this hospital, are greater than is shown by the reports of some of the most important hospitals in the cast. Ed. Reines, a negro, some days ago committed an assault upon a Miss Dora Langston, of Graves County, Ky., and made good his escape for the timebeing. He was pursued, however, by a body of men who were determined to lynch him if captured. Reines was finally arrested by the authorities in the lowlands of Ballard County, who started to Graves County jail with him. They were met on the way by a mob who immediately took possession of the prisoner and lynched him.

perry-mason-monroe-1881-08-22.A1:
Breaking a Planter's Neck.
NEW ORLEANS, LA., Aug. 19, 1881.—A special dispatch from Monroe, La., to the Democrat says: "Wednesday night, at the Kansas plantation, as Anderson Mitchell and his wife were walking along the road Mitchell was struck on the back of his neck with a stick, breaking his neck. He lived but a few minutes. Aaron Buder and Perry Munson, grocers, have been arrested on suspicion."

The Address of the Irish Revolutionary Convention.

PHILADELPHIA, August 23d.—The Ledger's New York special says: I hear from good authority that the British Consulate cabled the home Government the substance of the address of the so-called Irish Revolutionary Convention, which has been held in secret session here during the past few days; that the address, without the slightest qualification, proclaims an intention to destroy British vessels wherever they can be found, and declares that it is just as well to begin the work, which is most easy of accomplishment, and by the time a few English merchant vessels are destroyed the world may witness the beneficent sight of all the shipping merchants and insurance companies of England presenting a petition to Gladstone to reconsider the Irish question.

New York Politics—A Treaty of Peace.

NEW YORK, August 23d.—The Mayor and John Kelly are said to have made a treaty of peace, the first result of which will be the confirmation of the Mayor's nominees Tuesday. Mr. Grace and the ex-boss, it is said, were at Saratoga the other day, and some mutual friends improved the opportunity to bring them together to talk the thing over. The experiment proved a signal success, as both Barkises were willing. The basis of the treaty, it is understood, is an equitable division of the city patronage. In other words, a recognition of Tammany at the public crib.

The Vienna Boat Race—Base Treachery.

ITHACA (N. Y.), August 23d.—The Daily Journal says: Shinkels of the Cornell crew, Michael Casey, a saloon keeper, and Samuel W. Reed, a wholesale liquor dealer, made up a party that had agreed that Cornell should lose all the races abroad after the first—the Stewards', or Visitors'—which it was expected the crew would win. The Journal says there is documentary evidence of treachery, and states that Shinkel wrote Casey from London, before the Cornell crew had started for Vienna: "Bet that the Cornells will lose the Vienna race."

Fruit Warehouse Burned.

PHILADELPHIA, August 23d.—The fruit warehouse of Warner & Merritt, 50 and 54 North Delaware avenue, was burned to-day. Loss, $100,000; stock and machinery, $125,000; partially insured. Falling walls demolished several small adjoining buildings. The fire originated in an explosion of gas.

Freight Trains Trying to Pass Each Other on the Same Track.

RICHMOND (Va.), August 23d.—Two freight trains on the Richmond, Fredericksburg and Potomac Railroad came in collision at North Anna, and both were wrecked, interrupting travel. Engineer Carroll and a colored fireman are reported seriously injured.

The Signal Service.

CHEYENNE (Wy. T.), August 23d.—The Leader has information that a movement is progressing in official circles to have Vennor, of Canada, supersede Hazen as Chief of the Signal Service. Prominent military men and scientists are said to be interested.

Police Commissioners Removed.

NEW YORK, August 23d.—Mayor Grace to-day removed the Police Commissioners, after a trial on charges of failing to keep the streets clean. The Mayor has sent the Governor a long review of the testimony taken.

Not to be Removed.

WASHINGTON, August 23d.—The Commissioner of Indian Affairs, in view of the report of Inspector Haworth, will recommend the retention of Agent Eastman, of the Navajo Agency, New Mexico.

What Gambling Brings Men To.

CHICAGO, August 23d.—Charles Wright has been arrested here, charged with embuzzling $5,000 from Fred, S. Jones & Co., insurance agents, for whom he was cashier. He has confessed, attributing his fall to gambling.

Too Cheap to be Good.
New York, August 23d.—The Tribune reports the case of a man named Lautens selling to a carpenter named Jansen his (Lautens)' wife for $1. Mrs. Lautens had been unfaithful, and the bargain seemed to please all concerned.

Hotel Destroyed by Fire.
BUENA VISTA SPRINGS (Ky.), August 23d. The large frame hotel here is burned. The loss is heavy. The guests are being taken to neighboring farm houses.

More Negroes Lynched.
NEW ORLEANS, August 23d.—The Democrat's Monroe, La., special says: Early this morning unknown parties entered the jail, took out Perry Mason and Alex Wilson (colored), charged with murder, and hanged them.

Robbery of Jewelry.
ATLANTIC CITY, August 23d.—Mulligan's store was robbed to-night of $40,000 worth of jewelry.

Not Known in Chicago.
CHICAGO, August 23d.—No such person is known here as James S. Farwell, reported from San Francisco as being a native of Chicago, drowned there.

Business Portion of a Town Burned.
CHICAGO, August 23d.—The Inter-Ocean's Nakomis, Ill., special says: The little town of Raymond suffered the destruction by fire to-day of all the business portion. Loss, $35,000; insurance, $10,000.

The Water Famine at Richmond.
RICHMOND (VA.), August 23d.—The water famine continues. By order of the Mayor several mill dams will be cut, stopping the mills.

Resumed Work.
HORNELLSVILLE (N.Y.), August 23d.—The switchmen here resumed work at the old wages.

Ice and Coal Fire.
POUGHKEEPSIE (N. Y.), August 23d.—A fire at Barrytown to-day caused a loss of $53,000, mainly ice and coal.

MONROE, Aug. 23.—Between 1 and 2 o'clock this morning unknown parties entered the sheriff's office, broke open the desk where the keys of the jail were kept, obtained them, entered the jail and took Jerry Munson and Alex. Wilson, charged with murder, and hung them one and a half miles from town, Munson was charged with the murder of Anderson Mitchell on the 17th inst. Wilson was charged with the murder of Reuben Leonard, whom he called out of church and shot about a month ago.

EAGLE PASS, Aug. 23.—The large ferry-boat plying between here and Piedras Negras has been unable to cross the Rio Grande for some time, the river having been unusually high. Yesterday morning, the river having fallen somewhat, an attempt was made to cross. As the boat reached the middle of the stream, the tremendous rush of water threatened to swamp it, and the ferry-man cut the rope, holding the boat to the cable stretched across the river. Thus the occupants of the boat were temporarily saved from a watery grave to only be rapidly carried down the river by the rushing torrent. The helpless, rickety flatboat, with its terror-stricken-freight of five human beings, was soon lost to view. It is feared all are lost, as they have not been heard from up to this morning.

Captain Howgate has obtained bail and been released from custody.

The recent report that Breslau was to be placed in a state of siege is now denied.

Alsа Guthreaux, who was in jail at Toronto, for robbing the London and Paris jewelry store of $1,500 worth of jewelry, and who was admitted to bail in $2,500, has decamped. He was at one time civil sheriff of New Orleans.

T. B. Connery, managing editor of the New York Herald, retires on a pension, and Frank Lawley, of the London Telegraph, is coming over to succeed him. Chief Justice Gray is specially designated for the vacancy in the United States Supreme Court, as the New York Times points out, by the fact that he is that "rare character in our free republic, a man who, with ample means, devoted himself to the study of law, not for the purpose of practising as a counsellor, but with a sole view to becoming a learned jurist."

Guiteau, the President's assailant, had an encounter with one of the prison guards, who entered his cell Wednesday morning to compel obedience to the prison rules. Knocking down a man who said he hoped President Garfield would die, and getting fined for it, has proved a very profitable investment for Capt. Charles A. Cook, of Brownsville, O. Stupendous frauds have come to light in the management of the Kings County (N. Y.) Penitentiary during the past eight years. perry-mason-monroe-1881-08-22.A12:
Hanging by Judge Lynch.
Our community was startled and shocked on Tuesday morning last by the rumor, which proved to be founded on fact, that two of the prisoners in the jail had been taken from their cells on the previous night and hanged near the Bayou DeSiard road about two and a half miles from the court-house. These unfortunate parties were Alec Wilson, charged with the murder of Reuben Leonard and Perry Munson, charged with the murder of Anderson Mitchell—these, and their victims were all negroes. Both murders had been cold blooded and premeditated In the first case the victim was shot down at night and the other had his neck broken by a blow from a heavy bludgeon, whilst he was quietly walking on the roadside in company with his wife. In both cases the testimony against the prisoners was circumstantial but quite strong and convincing—still they had neither been proved guilty—and were both held in jail, subject to the investigation and action of the Grand Jury. The idea that our parish or its officers will arrest parties charged with the commission of crime and then fail to protect them is horrifying and revolting in the extreme. That a party of men can come to our parish seat, get possession of the jail keys, and without resistance commit such a crime as has startled our community this week as equally shameful and disgraceful. We trust and believe that the proper officers will investigate this matter to the bottom and make an example of all parties in any manner responsible for this barbarously cruel act.
perry-mason-monroe-1881-08-22.A14:
More Mob Law.
Monday night between 11 and 12 o'clock, a mob broke into the Sheriff's office, possessed themselves of the jail keys and carried off the bodies Alex Willson and Perry Munson, colored, both confined under charges of murder; the former for killing Reuben Leonard, colored, a month ago, and the latter for killing Anderson Mitchell, also colored, on the 17th instant. Willson had had a preliminary examination and had been committed without bail. Munson's examination was fixed for yesterday. The prisoners were hung between town and the Bayou DeSiard. Dr. Cage is the only person who saw the mob, and has no idea of its complexion. Some of them were evidently well acquainted with the Sheriff's office, as they knew just where to find the keys and what implements were necessary to force the locks. Such proceedings are indefensible and have and are doing the country infinite harm and injury.—Monroe Bulletin.

robert-barker-okolona-1881-07-30.A1: A brutal murder occurred at a colored church on the plantation of Mr. John Jolly, of this county, on Saturday night last. The particulars as we learn them were as follows: Luther White and Sam Robinson alias Rob Barker, seems to have been attracted by the same dam-sel, and it appears that White was the favorite. At any rate, on the night mentioned both men were at church, and when White emerged from the building Robinson who was standing by the door struck him with a heavy piece of wood breaking his skull and knocking him senseless. The murderer not satisfied with the deed, or not krowing he had already slain his victim, jumped upon his prostrate form, drew a knife and stabbed him to the heart. Those who witnessed the bloody deed were so horrified, that they were unable to collect their thoughts until the murderer arose to make his escape, and then their feeble efforts were not sufficient to detain him in his flight, and he made his escape. Up to this writing Robinson has not been arrested, but it is hoped Justice, swift, and sure, will ere long over-take him.

Seven Hundred of Them Going on a Picnic on the Atlantic Coast. New York Sun. The bark Ibis from Panacola, Jay vester-
The bark Ibis, from Pensacola, lay yesterday at the foot of Seventeenth street, North river. A Sun reporter boarded her and asked Captain Sawyer if he had really seen whales off Pimlico Sound on his way up the coast last Saturday.

"Whales?" said the genial Captain, "Any number of them. There must have been two miles of black backs and water-spouts."

Capt. Sawyer unrolled a time-worn chart on the table in his cabin and with his dividers followed down a number of pencil marks to latitude 40 degrees and longitude 74 degrees 15 minutes. This brought him to a point about eighty miles off Pimlico Sound, and further northeast of Cape Hatteras.

"It was on Saturday and Sunday, he continued, "when we encountered these sperm whales going south of southwest, as if to go around Hatteras. They were going very slowly, backs above the water, and were spouting all of the time. They were strolling along in groups, sunning themselves half an hour at a time, and then taking a header and coming up to spout."

"How many were there?"

"Well, first we met two schools of about 100 each, I should say. Occasionally they frolicked and flopped about heavily in a sort of dignified and elephantine sport. More followed, and the next morning (Sunday) we saw more. Altogether there were over 700 on the picnic. We passed within 500 feet of two big fellows, but they seemed preoccupied and didn't notice the ship. I don't think they knew we were there."

"Had you any means of capturing them?"

"No, and it did seem a pity to have so much valuable sperm oil indolently swimming away from us. There were some big whales there, too. I said to Limerick, one of my men here, 'Now there's a fellow that's worth $2000,' and he must have been, and there were bigger ones in the school. It would have been a harvest for a whaling ship. A million dollars in sperm whales is too good a haul to let go by, but we couldn't do anything. Occasionally I have seen a

sperm whale cruising along as far south as Savannah, and once in a while I've heard of whale ships off about there. But I never saw so many whales at one time before anywhere."

"Where were they going?"
"For squids, probably. That's a favorite food with them."

"Is there any danger to be feared from them?"
"No; they're harmless. I think I never heard of more than one case where a whale attacked a vessel, and that's in ancient history. Over a hundred years ago, I believe, the ship Easex was run down by a mad whale. My own experience with whales has been that they are shy, and if they upset a boat, do it by accident in trying to get away."

SENATOBIA, MISS.

Election of Delegates to the Democratic State Convention.

Special to the Appeal.

SENATOBIA, MISS., July 30.—The election for delegates to the Democratic Nominating Convention, which meets Monday, was held to-day. Everything passed off quietly.

The Republican Executive Committee met-day in the Courthouse, and appointed the 15th of August for a convention to nominate candidates for county offices.

OXFORD, MISS.

A Meeting of Dissatisfied Democrats and What Came of It.

Special to the Appeal.]

OXFORD, Miss., July 30.—The dissatisfied element of the Lafayette county Democracy met in mass-meeting here to-day. The crowd numbered about 200, 100 to 125 of whom participated in and approved of the meeting. A new set of delegates were appointed to go to Jackson with instructions to vote against Stone for Governor, and to vote for W. D. Holder for Auditor and E. H. Dial for Secretary of State. This new delegation, of course, will not be recognized by the State Convention.

A Greenback meeting was also held here to-day. An effort was made to get up a fusion with the Republicans, but the Republicans refused to nestle and bolted the meeting.

OKOLONA, MISS.

A Negro Murderer Lynched by a Mob of His Own Color.

OKOLONA, July 30.—About three weeks ago Robert Barker, colored, wilfully murdered Luther White, colored, about four miles from here. Barker went to White's house, and, without any notice or cause whatever, knocked him once or twice in the head with a club, spattering his brains over the floor. The murderer, not satisfied, then took his knife and ripped White's abdomen open. Barker has been at large until yesterday, when he was brought into town by a crowd that had been on the lookout for him ever since he committed the deed, and delivered to the proper authorities. To-day the officer, with a guard, started with him to the county jail in Houston, which is about twenty miles from here. When about six miles from town they were met by an armed mob, who seized the prisoner, carried him a short distance into the woods and shot him dead. Barker pleaded earnestly for his life, but without effect. Justice was meted out to him properly by men of his own color.

INDIAN ATROCITIES.

More Troops Needed to Protect the Frontier Ranchmen.

DENVER, July 30.—The Tribune's Las Vegas letter has the following on good authority: The Indians who attacked two packers near Alama Canon, on the 19th instant, have been followed ever since by Lieutenant Guilfoyle's command, which a day or two since surprised them in camp. After one hour's engagement the Indians fled, leaving the whole camp outfit, two horses and twelve mules in the possession of the soldiers. Two Indians are supposed killed and several wounded but were carried off. The Indians fled toward the Rio Grande, and are supposed to be bound for Old Mexico. They were direct from the Mescala agency, and numbered eleven bucks and one squaw.

Reliable news from Engle reports the burning of a ranche and a number of Mexicans and two unknown miners by the Indians near there.

It is thought there are three bands of Indians prowling about the country, as their signal fires were seen from Engle last night.

A San Marcial, New Mexico, special says two Mexicans and two miners were murdered between San Jose and Fort McCready by Indians, who are supposed to be heading from the Black Range. Company D, Ninth cavalry, has been ordered upon a scout from Ojo Caliente. Chief Name will probably co-operate with Mescaleros if he is aware they are on the war path.

robert-barker-okolona-1881-07-30.A4: Our readers will remember that we published some weeks since an account of the cruel and inhuman murder of Luther White by Rob. Barker. Since the killing of White it seems Barker has been prowling around the neighborhood with the avowed intention of killing three or four other persons. When this was accomplished he proposed to flee the country. On last Friday evening the quiet of the city was disturbed by the entrance of at least one hundred armed men, mostly colored, who had the desperado in charge, and delivered him over to the officers of the law. Barker was at once put in jail and closely guarded on Friday night, and Saturday morning was brought before the Mayor, where he waved an examination, and was committed to jail. The jail here not being secure, Officer Buford was instructed to carry the prisoner to Houston for confinement. Early in the morning a large crowd of people assembled in town, and it was evident much excitement prevailed among them, and some suqdued threats of lynching were made. The officers were aware of this, and knew full well the only safety for the prisoner was to get him out of town immediately, and if possible without the knowledge of the infuriated populace. This they endeavored to do, but the sequel showed without success. The lynchers kept a close lookout, and were fully aware of all the movements made. Indeed it seems that a party of near one hundred stationed themselves on the road about five miles from town, at what is known as Shaw creek bottom and patiently waited the arrival of the posse, while a large number followed the officer and his charge from town. When they arrived at Shaw creek, the signal was given and twenty or thirty colored men jumped into the road and demanded the criminal. Resistance was worse than useless, and Officer Buford could do nothing more than beg for the life of the culprit and enter his protest against the unlawful act. The mob did not parley but seized the bridle of the mule upon which Barker was mounted, hurried him into the thicket, and before the officer could hitch his horse and follow to the place of execution, the report of twenty guns told the fate of the murderer. After the shooting the crowd dispersed as if by magic, and the slayer of three men, was left a lifeless, mangled mass upon the ground. We do not approve of mob law, but there can be no doubt, that the victim in this case received a justly merited punishment, and we trust it may prove a warning deter others as vicious from crime
robert-barker-okolona-1881-07-30.A5: JUDGING from the numerous cases, which have occurred within the past few years, the negro Rob. Barker would have made a saint in glory, if the wicked mob that shot him to death had only given him time to repent and be converted. In other other words, had he been incarcerated in jail, brought to trial and sentenced to expiate his heinous crime on the scaffold, the pious labors of the zealous ministry, who bank so heavily on the historic "thief on the cross," would have converted his dark soul and sent him shouting to the Heavenly paradise. The action of the Lynchers was hard on Barker, but we console ourselves with the reflection that the society of Saints and Angels is not to be contaminated with his presence.

Batesville Blade: On Thursday morning, 22h inst., a young negro boy, the son of Matilda Lard, received a terrible castigation from his mother for stealing. It appears that the boy last Wednesday stole fifty cents from his sister and the same day received a terrible beating which, it seems, and little effect in correcting his bad habits, for the following day he stole a box of bluing from a white lady. For this last offense the boy's mother put him in what is known as a "grass sack" and set fire to it. The boy was badly burned about the body, neck and arms, and complains of internal pains, caused by inhaling flames. The boy suffers intense pain and his condition is critical.

Crystal Springs Monitor: Mr. Thos. Finlay, a farmer residing near Georgetown, this county, shot and killed a negro named Will Cato, on the former's plantation last Tuesday morning. The negro, it is stated, and abused Mr. Finlay's wife, during that gentleman's absence from home; and, on his return, finding the negro on his premises, asked for an explanation, when the negro advanced upon him in a threatening manner, when Mr. Finlay shot him. The verdict of the coroner's jury was: "Came to his death by gun-shot wounds from unknown hands." It is reported that considerable excitement exists among the blacks in the neighborhood. Mr. Finlay does not deny shooting the negro, and told some of his friends that he would surrender himself to the officers of the law within a few days.
